sections.title: CONCLUSION
sections.text_preview: A 4-MB L2 Cache was integrated with a 64-bit 1.6-GHz RISC Microprocessor. The technology used a 90-nm node transistor with eight layers of metal. Common write and read circuits were used for Data, Tag, and LRU L2 cache blocks. references.sentence: The physical location of the Tag/LRU blocks are interleaved between the CPU core and the Data cache array to optimize the hit signal critical path (see the photomicrograph in Fig. 1 and the ﬂoorplan in Fig. 2).

Registers are located at the CPU/L2 cache boundary, at the edge between the Tag/LRU and the Data cache array, at the input to the memory McINTYRE et al.: A 4-MB ON-CHIP L2 CACHE FOR A 90-nm 1.6-GHz 64-bit MICROPROCESSOR TABLE I CHIP FEATURES AND ATTRIBUTES Fig. 1.

The physical location of the Tag/LRU blocks are interleaved between the CPU core and the Data cache array to optimize the hit signal critical path (see the photomicrograph in Fig. 1 and the ﬂoorplan in Fig. 2).
The CPU clock is distributed to the data cache memory array edge, as well as to the Tag/LRU arrays horizontally (Fig. 2).

Select SD, SR, and SW block selects, which control respectively decode, read, and write, are derived from the CPU clock (Figs. 2 and 3), with the clock edge in each case adjusted in half-cpu clock cycle increments to enable subarray operation without further use of the clock.
The tradeoffs were acceptable given design schedule requirements and veriﬁcation constraints. 53 Fig. 2.
Each sub-array maintains 57 one column-redundant element containing all ways—each column has a group of four bitline pairs located within the sub-array (Fig. 2; note four sections per cluster).
(Registers in Fig. 3 without a clock connection use the CPU clock.) This method accommodates the pipeline, allowing separate writes and reads simultaneously to separate sub-blocks.
A minimum of six ﬂoorplan-dependent pipeline delays are required (Fig. 3) to read or write the cache.
Bits per bitline were reduced to 256, with a small impact to array efﬁciency, in order to insure adequate array access. 54 Fig. 3.
